title: Energy is conserved because physics doesn’t change over time
body: In 1918 the mathematician Emmy Noether proved that whenever the laws of physics stay the same under a smooth change, such as shifting in time, moving in space or rotating, some quantity must be conserved. So conservation of energy, momentum and angular momentum aren’t separate lucky rules; they follow from symmetries of nature. Her theorem became a cornerstone of modern physics, where new laws are often found by hunting for symmetries.

steps.label: Choose a shift in time or space, or a turn
Check: do the laws stay the same?
If yes, something must be conserved
Time gives energy, space gives momentum

slides.heading: Time → energy
slides.text: The laws of physics work the same today as tomorrow. That symmetry in time is exactly what makes energy a conserved quantity.

slides.heading: Space → momentum
slides.text: The laws are the same here as anywhere else. That symmetry under shifting position is why momentum is conserved.

slides.heading: Rotation → spin
slides.text: No direction in space is special, so angular momentum is conserved. It’s why a spinning skater speeds up when pulling their arms in.

slides.heading: A cosmic catch
slides.text: An expanding universe isn’t the same from moment to moment, so physicists note that total energy isn’t simply conserved on cosmic scales.

slides.question: Which symmetry of nature gives us conservation of momentum?
options: Same laws at every moment in time
Same laws at every place in space
slides.explanation: Noether’s theorem pairs each symmetry with a conserved quantity: shifting in time gives energy, shifting in space gives momentum, and rotating gives angular momentum.

slides.heading: Match the symmetry to what it conserves
slides.explanation: Emmy Noether proved in 1918 that every smooth symmetry of the laws of physics comes with a conserved quantity.
